title_original: Mouse Co-Director Alex Thompson On Crafting One Of The Year’s Best Hidden Gems

blocks.text: A day before I was meant to meet Alex Thompson, co-director of Mouse alongside his creative partner Kelly O’Sullivan, I saw a thought I’d been having for months articulated on Indiewire . “ Mouse Is One of the Year’s Best Movies,” the headline accurately stated, “Why Aren’t More People Talking About It?” After premiering to great acclaim at the beginning of the year, Mouse is now playing in U.S. theaters, yet the movie seems to have slipped through the cracks of awards-season fluff and online movie chatter. Of the barrage of FYC emails I’ve been receiving lately, Mouse has been conspicuous for its relative absence.

“I think there’s something refreshing about having that conversation out in the open a little bit. Though, of course, I’m extremely bashful about being the one doing the talking,” Thompson judiciously explains to me in his hotel lobby, fresh from the airport at the Thessaloniki Film Festival where he’s arrived to continue a rollout that began in Berlin back in February. “I make movies with about five producers, who are all doing different things, from setting up tables at crafty to pushing financing through. And all we’re talking about is: How do we define success for this movie? Where is the right launchpad? Where is the right home? People talk about strategy, but it’s kind of all bullshit.”

Thompson and O’Sullivan (who are married and have a kid) broke onto the scene with Saint Frances in 2019 and went two-for-two with Ghostlight a few years later. For Mouse fans, that movie was also significant for marking their first collaboration with Catherine and Tara Mullen, a real mother and daughter acting duo who both returned for Thompson and O’Sullivan’s latest—with Catherine (brilliant) starring as Minnie, a girl entering her final year in high school who strikes up a friendship with the more affluent mother (Okenedo) of her recently deceased friend; and Tara playing Barbara, her sometimes brusque and harried but never less than loving mom.

Funny, bittersweet, refreshingly spiky, and brought home on a beautifully lilting score by the Walkmen’s Hamilton Leithauser, it struck me on first watch in Berlin as the best film of its kind since Lady Bird , an opinion that has held firm on second viewing. For roughly half an hour, we spoke about Okenedo’s magic, early-2000s needle drops, and how best to avoid low-hanging fruit.

The Film Stage: With Tara and Catherine, who are just incredible together in this movie, I know you worked together on Ghostlight . Did you or Kelly write their roles in this film with them specifically in mind?

Alex Thompson: No, not at all. Kelly wrote Mouse in 2019, before Ghostlight and immediately after Saint Frances , but because that financing got scuttled, we pivoted. Kelly had Ghostlight ready to go. It was during the SAG and writers’ strikes, but Kelly was eight months pregnant. So we ended up getting our waiver because I sent them an email saying, “If we push one more week, she will give birth.” And then we got it.
So she wrote that part for Keith [Kupferer]. And he was like, “I have a daughter. She’d love to audition.” And Catherine [turned out to be] a generational talent.

She’s unreal. And to think that Helen wasn’t written with Sophie Okonedo in mind is incredible, too. It’s such a perfect role for her. That blend of toughness and warmth, and with a little spikiness in there as well.
The funny thing is that I always felt—and Kelly would probably disagree—that on the page, Helen felt very cool. So you think of certain actors who can project that kind of coolness and reserve.
Which would naturally be very impressive to a girl like Minnie.

Yeah, and Sophie was someone at the top of my list. I liked that she evokes the 2000s— Dirty Pretty Things , you know? She evokes that era and is iconic. She’s also an all-timer as far as theater work goes. She brings so much humor, sparkle, and mischief. When she comes into the girls’ room at the beginning and almost gets into bed with them, saying, “I’m going to stay with you,” you understand why Minnie wants to be in this house with this mum.

And Sophie isn’t thinking about any of it. I remember so many times saying, “I loved it when you did that in the last take,” and she’d reply, “Oh, great. I don’t know what I did. I don’t know why I did it.” She’s just brilliant.
Did she and Catherine find that rhythm together?

I assumed that, because of Sophie’s pedigree, there would be a kind of mentor-mentee energy on set. Sophie is the veteran of the arts, and we’re all going to appreciate what she brings and learn a thing or two, but pretty quickly, everyone folded into the ensemble. That doesn’t mean they disappeared in any way. They all understood that everyone was important, and they would all speak up and assert themselves in their own way. I don’t think I realized how good Sophie and Catherine would be together. They ended up being so suited for one another in their acting styles. Catherine, similarly, is someone who turns the faucet on and sees what comes out. And a small adjustment can cascade into a totally different performance.

I’ve made two films since Mouse , and both have this sort of thing that Ghostlight had: there’s a secret, degrees of revelation, a catharsis and a climax, and by the end you know everything. Mouse isn’t like that. You know everything from page one. The characters are barely hiding what they’re feeling. They can’t.
I think Barbara gets to have a bit of an arc, no?
Barbara does. It’s funny, because I’m so familiar with the script that I’ve only recently realized it’s a reveal that, essentially, she’s a great mum.
I think it’s because, at first, you only see her through Minnie’s eyes. And then her last scene at the variety show is just—
Yeah, she fights for her. I love that last scene because we get Barbara being there with her daughter, but we also get to see her cowed by Helen’s very righteous anger and pain.
She’s so good in that scene.

Yeah. It was a crazy scene. We shot it for five hours—basically three shots, two cameras. It was crazy. We didn’t lay marks, so the actors were just feeling the space. It was really an uncommon approach. I understand it comes from having an essentially linear story that just gets to exist. And it’s understating the fact that, for that to be successful, it has to be this really muscular thing on the page as well.

There are some beautiful details that you just leave hanging there. I’m thinking of this baby in Minnie’s house, who we learn Barbara has essentially adopted from a troubled home. There’s a whole world in that detail, about class, and how having a baby means different things in different circumstances. We get one scene when Helen learns about it, and get to think about what’s going through Helen’s head, and then it’s just there, and you leave it. I wouldn’t change a thing, but were you tempted to add another scene?

Minnie used to be quite mean to Dustin, actually. We took that out because we realized it wasn’t about him. Something I talk about a lot is that characters don’t need to say what they actually feel. If they’re articulating their point of view too well, you can feel the screenwriter. We talk a bit about how, if there are too many details, the audience can get confused. But there’s something about seeing all the animals and then seeing Dustin. He feels like he’s of a piece with all these strays.
And that’s our son. He’s a discovery. [Laughs]
Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson on the set of Mouse
I also love how, in that variety show scene, the annoying girls end up being the best act. Like that’s just life sometimes, you know? Tough shit.

That’s the promise and challenge of the script. It’s described as something that’s surprisingly moving, but to Helen it’s not that. She’s going to be moved by the thing that isn’t the thing we’re supposed to be focused on. Only now have I realized that the power of Minnie’s song, which is about 40 seconds long, comes from the audience being given permission to feel all those big movie feelings in the moments before, with “Time After Time” and Cyndi Lauper and these girls.

Because they give us that, we can feel satisfied by those 40 seconds of effort and struggle, and have our regrets afterwards. But if it weren’t for them, it would all be on Minnie. I love that some things are moving and you can’t pick the things that move us.
Are there any lines of dialogue you’re particularly fond of? I loved Minnie’s line near the start, “How can I forget you? You take up too much space.”

I’m a big fan of characters we love being unkind. I think it says so much in those moments, and I actually love that line of dialogue. When I was in high school, I did theater. I remember one of the women I admired was in Tartuffe with me. She played the maid, who either had no lines or very few lines, and I played Valère, who had a lot of lines. I was a freshman and she was a senior. One day backstage, I remember saying something like, “Are you off-book yet?” It was like me trying to assert that I wasn’t just a freshman, you know. But in the process, I could tell I’d hurt her feelings. It’s funny how quick and easy it is to be unkind. When Minnie says that, it’s both true and not true, because we’re going to see for 90 minutes exactly how much space gets left behind when you lose somebody.

The confluence of events is so weird, but Kelly’s mum passed away when we were shooting. Then we shot another movie last year, and my grandmother, whose house we were filming around, passed away basically as soon as we wrapped. We were a week into post. She was someone I remember getting annoyed by sometimes. But I want to have the right to be annoyed. I want them in my life to be annoyed at.
The music choices are really great throughout. You get a lot of bangers from that era. I loved hearing Lit’s “My Own Worst Enemy” at the pool party.

I’m very proud of the music because this whole movie was directed, I would say, defensively. With Saint Frances , for example, Nate Kerseller, the DP, and I were like, “We have to get out of the way of the script.” It’s an abortion movie, you’re a male director. Get out of the way of the script. Don’t try to put the Alex Thompson spin on it. Just get the fuck out of the way of the script.

We developed this visual language that we carried into Rounding and Ghostlight . It was designed not to gild the lily emotionally, and to avoid any moments where the audience would feel manipulated, even though that is itself a form of manipulation. We want people to feel things, but I believe they won’t if they feel our fingers on the scale.
For this kind of story and the themes, you’ve got almost no low-hanging fruit, I think. Or at least, it’s saved for very late, like the grief meeting that Helen eventually attends.

That meeting scene, it was shot on documentary lenses by Luke and Nate, who also shot Ren Faire . Nate was the DP on that, and Luke was the operator, and the way they shot that is so fucking insane. But that’s their world. So I said, “We’re going to hold a grief group, and Sophie’s going to be in it, but we’re not going to engage with them, we’re not going to set up close-ups, and we’re not going to tell her to do anything.”

And Sophie, I think she was nervous that day because she may have been worried about some expectation from us. I’m always worried when I come to a scene and think, “Ah, we really need to hit something here emotionally.” Because that means you’re no longer looking for what’s exciting. You’re no longer discovering or playing with chemistry. You’re trying to make something happen, and that often feels affected. And in that scene, she says nothing. She doesn’t engage in the improvisation that everyone else is doing. And they are all real grieving parents.
I was actually curious about that.

Yeah, the moderator, the grief-group leader, was a real grief leader, and the people had all been in a group together. She got them all back together to lead a discussion about their kids and families. And the craziest thing happened: as we were setting up, Barry Clifton, who plays the guy who greets her at the coffee table, he said, “You know, I lost my son 20 years ago. I didn’t know this was what this was going to be. Is it okay if I speak?”

And we were like, “Yeah, as much as you feel comfortable with.” He ended up being a fulcrum in that scene. He has some of the most stirring moments, and it all happened organically. We saw it, and I said, “We’ve got to keep this in the edit.” We realised we wanted to consciously disrupt the cinematic continuity for the audience. Like, you’re watching a movie, but this is also real. Sophie is being caught off-guard in that room.
The movie does a great job of evoking the era without it taking up too much space. What was your and Kelly’s approach regarding that aspect of it?
With the time period, we didn’t want it to feel like a movie about a time period. We looked mostly at Kelly’s high school photos and some art photography from that time.
There are some great era-specific gags. When Brad tells Minnie that he’s gonna enlist to “go get Osama.” The Britney/Christina convo.
Oh, yeah, and Shaggy at the funeral.
Hilarious. And weirdly plausible. I could easily imagine some high school kids back then doing something like that.

And that came about because of how long it took after the first Sundance rejection. We went home for Christmas, watched Love Actually , and Liam Neeson’s character plays a video montage to “Bye Bye Baby.”
Another grieving character.
He is, and it’s this sort of ridiculous moment. I realised, “Oh, this has to be Shaggy. It has to be Shaggy.”
And what about this Hamilton Litehauser score? It’s like note-perfect melancholy. Never lays it on too thick.

It’s wonderful, and he came out of the delivery room fully formed with that thing. We had a full score made by our collaborator, Queen Simon, who did Saint Frances , Rounding , and Ghostlight . But it just didn’t quite thread the needle. So rather than try to wrestle it into something, we decided to start totally from scratch. And Hamilton, of course, is a brilliant pianist, and he just spun out this perfect note of harmony, expression, and melancholy, as you said. I think melancholy is one of the best tones for a film score.
Before we wrap up, I just wanted to ask: have you seen Clarissa , Sophie’s other big film this year? What a lovely thing, to have these two films arrive in each other’s slipstream.
No, I haven’t. But I met those filmmakers, and they’re such wonderful people. I’m so excited to see it.
What stage are you at with The Steel Harp ?
It’s complete. We’re just hoping to have a festival premiere to announce soon. And the next one after that is in the editing phase. We just did pick-ups yesterday.
The Steel Harp is another story about a younger and older woman, is that correct?

The Steel Harp definitely is, yeah. Though more than slightly older. It’s Lois Smith, who’s in her 90s, and Cherry Jones is in there. And then the next one after that is Body of Work , with Catherine and Carrie Coon.
Looking forward to seeing it.
Yeah, I’ll have to make sure it’s good.
Mouse is now in theaters.
